analysis.one_liner: Extends clean energy and efficiency tax credits while ending tax breaks for oil and gas companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in November 2015 and died there when the Congress ended, with 21 supporters, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend more than a dozen expiring tax credits through 2016: credits for homeowners who make their houses more energy efficient, buyers of fuel-cell vehicles, builders of energy-efficient homes, and producers of renewable electricity and biodiesel. It would also create new credits for things like waste-heat power and community wind projects. To help cover the cost, it would repeal a long list of tax preferences for oil and gas companies, including write-offs for drilling costs, credits for marginal wells, and special accounting rules for the biggest integrated oil companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who install insulation, efficient windows, or efficient heating equipment would get an extended tax credit that, under the bill, would also cover installation labor. Buyers of fuel-cell vehicles, builders of energy-efficient new homes, and businesses making efficient commercial buildings would get extended credits. Renewable electricity, biodiesel, and small biodiesel producers would keep their credits, and new categories like waste-heat recovery and community wind projects would qualify. Taxpayers generally would gain from the repeal of oil and gas tax preferences.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homeowners, clean energy firms, biodiesel producers

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the nonbusiness energy property credit through 2016 and adds installation labor costs to the covered expenses, so homeowners making efficiency upgrades get more of their actual cost back.

It extends credits for fuel cell motor vehicles, alternative fuel refueling property, energy-efficient new homes, energy-efficient commercial buildings, and renewable electricity production through 2016.

It creates new investment tax credits for waste-heat-to-power property and community wind projects up to 20 megawatts, and authorizes up to $2.7 billion in additional advanced energy manufacturing tax credits.

Title III repeals or restricts oil and gas tax preferences, including the intangible drilling cost deduction, percentage depletion, credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery, the domestic production deduction for oil and gas, LIFO accounting for major integrated oil companies, and limits on foreign tax credits for companies paying foreign levies in exchange for economic benefits.
It extends and reforms biodiesel tax credits, moving them to a producer-based credit with a 10-cent-per-gallon boost for small producers on their first 15 million gallons.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, from small marginal-well operators to the largest integrated producers, would lose the tax preferences the bill repeals. The federal Treasury would also bear the cost of the extended clean energy credits; the record contains no cost estimate showing whether the oil and gas repeals fully offset them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies; the Treasury

drawbacks.text: The bill extends more than a dozen tax credits, and no cost estimate appears in the record, so it is unknown whether the oil and gas repeals fully pay for the extensions.
One provision would let renewable energy and fuel projects operate as publicly traded partnerships, a tax structure that primarily benefits large investors in those projects.

The oil and gas repeal provisions would raise the tax burden on domestic producers, including operators of marginal wells that the current credits were designed to keep in production; critics of such repeals argue this raises production costs and could reduce domestic output.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is structured as a trade: extend consumer and clean energy credits, paid in part by ending tax preferences that oil and gas companies have held for decades. The consumer-facing provisions are modest in dollar terms but directly reach households, and including installation labor in the efficiency credit helps the workers who do the installations. The main weaknesses are the absence of any published cost estimate and a provision that benefits wealthy investors in energy partnerships. On balance it weighs in favor of ordinary households, but it never received any committee or floor consideration, so its actual costs and design were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2015 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on November 17, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
The bill had 20 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no Republican support.
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept every tax preference the bill would have repealed. Clean energy industries, biodiesel producers, and homeowners got no extended credits from this bill, though Congress did extend many similar credits in other legislation later in 2015.

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 20 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 17, 2015 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has long lobbied against repeal of its tax preferences, including drilling write-offs and depletion allowances, which this bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would repeal a long list of their tax preferences, including intangible drilling cost deductions, percentage depletion, marginal well and enhanced oil recovery credits, the domestic production deduction, and LIFO accounting for major integrated companies. Their gain from keeping these breaks comes at taxpayers' expense, so their interest in the bill ran against the public's.

Extended production and investment credits, new waste-heat and community wind credits, $2.7 billion in additional manufacturing credits, and publicly traded partnership status would all expand their business. Households benefit from cheaper clean energy and efficiency upgrades, though some provisions primarily benefit large investors.
Extended $1-per-gallon credits with a bonus for small producers, funded by requiring the fuel to be produced in the United States. Cheaper, domestically produced biodiesel benefits fuel buyers.

Extended credits for energy-efficient new homes and, for the first time in this bill, counting installation labor toward the homeowner efficiency credit, which puts more work and pay in contractors' hands while lowering homeowners' energy bills.
